title: A manufacturable room-temperature superconductor at ambient pressure

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an identifiable bulk material that superconducts near 300 K at approximately 1 bar, remains stable outside its synthesis apparatus, and can be reproducibly manufactured and shaped into useful components. Superconductivity would be established through both resistance-free electrical transport and the characteristic magnetic response, including Meissner flux expulsion. The target therefore combines a physical property with chemical stability and practical fabrication.

Scope synthesis: high-pressure synthesis followed by recovery could qualify, provided the recovered material retains the required properties at ambient pressure. Continuous diamond-anvil confinement would not qualify. Production beyond microgram quantities and shaping while preserving superconductivity are part of the intended innovation; detecting a transition in a microscopic specimen would establish only part of that capability.

significance.text: A stable, processable room-temperature superconductor could provide resistance-free conductors and superconducting magnetic components without liquid cryogens or extreme operating pressures. Removing those constraints could substantially change power transmission, generators and magnetic technologies such as MRI. The supplied reports illustrate why temperature alone is insufficient: a material operating near room temperature under roughly 250 GPa still requires an extraordinary pressure apparatus.

Conditional impact synthesis: changes to electrical infrastructure and magnets could be comparable in historical importance to the transistor's effect on switching. That comparison expresses the potential breadth of applications, rather than a demonstrated forecast or a claim that superconductivity performs the transistor's function. Benefits for some computing hardware are also plausible downstream possibilities, contingent on suitable devices and system architectures.

Engineering synthesis: superconductivity near 300 K would not by itself establish commercial usefulness. Conductors must carry useful currents, magnets must tolerate useful magnetic fields, and components must survive fabrication and service. Wire or tape manufacture, joints, device integration, durability and cost would still require engineering. Resistance-free transport also does not imply that an entire electrical system has no energy losses.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central scientific challenge is to obtain a composition and crystal structure that supports superconductivity near room temperature while remaining stable at ambient pressure. The supplied hydride work illustrates the gap: it reports high transition temperatures under extreme compression, acknowledges difficulties determining hydrogen positions, and describes instability on decompression. Establishing which phase actually produces the superconducting response is essential to making and improving it reproducibly.

Recovery and persistence are separate barriers from achieving a high transition temperature. The pressure-quench result described by Science News concerns a claimed 151 K transition at atmospheric pressure, with retention for at least three days at 77 K and deterioration around 200 K. A recovered state that survives cold storage but deteriorates on warming does not establish a stable room-temperature material.

Manufacturing synthesis: a successful route must produce repeatable quantities of the same superconducting phase, control composition and phase purity, and preserve performance when the material is shaped into components. The hydride manuscript describes specimens approximately 10–20 μm across, illustrating the distance between the reported experimental scale and macroscopic manufacture. Those dimensions do not establish a specimen mass; the microgram language defines the proposed manufacturing target rather than a measured mass in that experiment.

Diagnostic barriers also remain distinct from manufacturing barriers. Transport measurements, magnetic measurements and structural characterization answer different questions: whether resistance vanishes, whether the material exhibits the expected superconducting magnetic response, and which composition and structure carry that response. The hydride authors report transport evidence while leaving direct Meissner characterization for future work, and the pressure-quench news report identifies an explicit zero-resistance demonstration as missing.

current_state.text: Song, Ma and colleagues' preprint, revised October 6, 2025, reports superconducting onset temperatures of 271–298 K at 195–266 GPa in material assigned to hexagonal LaSc2H24. The manuscript reports zero resistance and suppression of the transition by an applied magnetic field. These are the authors' reported results in microscopic, pressure-confined specimens; they do not demonstrate a recovered, manufacturable ambient-pressure superconductor. An onset temperature identifies the beginning of a transition and should not be treated as proof of zero resistance at that same temperature.

The preprint acknowledges limitations in resolving the positions of hydrogen atoms and leaves direct Meissner measurements for future work. In its November 7, 2025 coverage, Physics World describes the pressures as comparable to those at Earth's centre and reports Sven Friedemann's concern that more comprehensive diffraction measurements are needed to attribute superconductivity securely to the proposed structure. That concern addresses phase identification; it does not independently establish that the reported electrical transition is false.

The supplied review describes both an abstract landing page and manuscript text covering all 41 pages for the hydride preprint, while retaining a partial-access or extraction qualification. The plots, diffraction figures and other figure images were not inspected in that review. Consequently, the supplied evidence supports an account of the manuscript's claims and acknowledged limitations, but not an independent assessment of the quality of its graphical evidence.

Emily Conover's March 9, 2026 Science News report describes a pressure-quench claim of superconductivity at 151 K and atmospheric pressure in HgBa2Ca2Cu3O8+δ, also called Hg-1223. It presents a possible ambient-pressure temperature record conditionally, pending confirmation, and reports that the experiment did not explicitly demonstrate zero resistance. The reported retained state lasted at least three days at 77 K and deteriorated around 200 K. Neither the claimed transition temperature nor the reported stability reaches the proposed room-temperature operating target.

The pressure-quench account is available here through Science News, which identifies the Deng and colleagues PNAS study. No primary PNAS text is supplied for direct assessment. Its absence limits evaluation of the experiment; it does not establish that the result is false or verify the earlier assertion that retrieval failed. The news report's discussion of confirmed records and the hydride preprint's higher claimed onset temperatures concern different levels of evidentiary confirmation and should not be conflated.

Science News reports that earlier room-temperature superconductivity claims did not hold up, but the supplied evidence does not specifically establish the history of LK-99. The dated sources describe substantial remaining barriers through March 2026. They do not establish the field's complete status through November 1, 2026, so this record makes no claim that all subsequent developments have been checked.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent groups should synthesize the same identified phase and reproduce zero resistance together with a Meissner response at approximately 1 bar above 290 K. The 290 K figure is a proposed minimum demonstration threshold, not an established standard or a sufficient operating margin for every room-temperature environment. Measurements should distinguish the onset of a transition from the temperature at which zero resistance is demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Independent zero-resistance and Meissner replication above 290 K near 1 bar

completion_criteria.text: Proposed identification and replication requirements: determine composition and crystal structure with enough confidence to associate the superconducting response with the same phase across specimens and laboratories. Transport, magnetic and structural evidence should converge, addressing the possibility that a minor or unidentified phase produces the observed signal. Repeated syntheses should establish reproducibility beyond a single successful specimen.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible synthesis links superconductivity to an identified composition and structure

completion_criteria.text: Proposed stability and manufacturing requirements: retain the superconducting state in macroscopic specimens outside the synthesis cell, without continuous anvil confinement; reproducibly produce quantities beyond the microgram scale; and shape the material into a useful form while preserving its properties. High-pressure synthesis is compatible with these criteria if the recovered material operates at ambient pressure. Stability should be tested at the intended operating temperature, rather than inferred from cold storage.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible macroscopic fabrication preserves superconductivity outside the synthesis cell

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical characterization: report the temperature, current and magnetic-field ranges over which performance persists, along with retention time, environmental conditions and changes after fabrication or repeated operation. These measurements would define demonstrated usefulness for particular applications. Finite tests establish reproducibility and breadth within tested conditions; they cannot establish unlimited lifetime, universal manufacturability or suitability for every electrical technology.
completion_criteria.label: Report operating ranges and durability under tested environmental conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-09, phase-pure synthesis of arbitrary designed crystalline solids, has the closest materials overlap. Reliable control of a chosen superconducting phase could help realize CHEMREV-03. The targets remain distinct: CHEMREV-03 requires one practically useful material with exceptional superconducting properties, while CHEMREV-09 seeks broad control over designed crystalline solids and does not itself guarantee those properties.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-01, predicting realistic chemical outcomes before experiment, could help identify candidate compositions, structures and synthesis conditions. Predictive success would assist discovery but would not replace synthesis, superconductivity measurements, recovery or fabrication. CHEMREV-04, practical on-demand synthesis of arbitrary stable molecules, concerns a broader molecular synthesis capability; it does not automatically supply a bulk crystalline phase with the required collective electronic behaviour.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-10, positional chemical manufacture of macroscopic, atomically specified matter, overlaps through precise composition, structure and manufacturing control. Such control could help make a selected superconducting material, but it would not establish that the selected arrangement superconducts near room temperature. Conversely, a manufacturable superconductor could be achieved through conventional bulk processing without attaining general atomically specified manufacture.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-08, an air-breathing battery with aviation-relevant specific energy, shares a potential role in improved electrical systems but addresses energy storage. CHEMREV-03 concerns conduction and magnetic behaviour. Success in either would not establish the other's performance target, and possible benefits within a shared system do not merge the two innovations.

Metallic hydrogen is a possible scientific route rather than a separate entry in the supplied roster. The hydride manuscript distinguishes proposed superconductivity in metallic hydrogen from experimental evidence of metallization. Metallization, superconductivity near room temperature and recovery into a stable, processable ambient-pressure material are separate achievements. Metallic hydrogen would overlap with this innovation only if it delivered the required superconducting and practical properties.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish developments after March 2026 through November 1, 2026.

The hydride's structural assignment, direct Meissner response and independent reproducibility remain unresolved within the supplied evidence; the review did not inspect its plots or diffraction figures.
The review retains a partial-extraction qualification for the hydride manuscript despite describing text covering all 41 pages; the record does not resolve that qualification further.
The primary PNAS pressure-quench paper is absent, preventing direct assessment of its experimental details and superconductivity diagnostics.
The pressure-quench result's independent confirmation, explicit zero-resistance evidence and longer-term stability remain unresolved here.
The supplied record does not verify the LK-99-specific history or the purported opposing April 2026 replication reports.
No material-specific evidence supplied here establishes scalable fabrication, useful current and magnetic-field limits, durability or cost for the proposed room-temperature capability.
The proposed 290 K threshold and other completion requirements are editorial proposals; application-specific operating margins and acceptance thresholds remain to be defined.

brief.title: Practical resistance-free wires at room temperature
possible: Power lines could carry electricity without electrical resistance at room temperature and ordinary air pressure. The material could be made repeatedly and shaped into wires or other useful components.
Hospitals could use superconducting magnets in magnetic resonance imaging scanners without liquid cooling agents. Generators and other magnetic equipment could use them too.
why: Removing extreme cooling and pressure requirements could make resistance-free conductors and powerful magnets useful much more widely. That could change how electricity suppliers transmit power and how manufacturers build generators and medical scanners.

sources.who: L. Deng, Paul Chu and colleagues
sources.showed: They reported signs of superconductivity up to 151 K at ordinary pressure after rapidly releasing compression. The result awaits confirmation and did not explicitly demonstrate zero resistance.

shown: Song, Ma and colleagues report a transition beginning near room temperature, plus zero resistance, in microscopic samples under extreme pressure. Their work remains a preprint, and the beginning of the transition does not establish zero resistance at that temperature.
Deng and colleagues report signs of superconductivity at ordinary pressure up to 151 K after rapid pressure release. The material retained its properties in cold storage but deteriorated on warming.
missing: Independent teams have yet to reproduce both zero resistance and magnetic field expulsion near room temperature at ordinary pressure.
The composition and atomic structure responsible for the response need a firm, reproducible identification.
A material must remain superconducting outside its synthesis equipment at room temperature and survive manufacture into useful components.
Useful current capacity, magnetic-field tolerance and durability still need demonstration.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation at ordinary pressure above 290 K
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to reproduce zero resistance and the Meissner response, which expels magnetic fields, above 290 K at ordinary pressure. Together these would establish superconductivity under the target conditions.

milestones.label: Repeated synthesis identifies the material responsible
milestones.explanation: Repeated experiments across laboratories would have to link superconductivity to the same composition and atomic structure. That would establish which material must be made reliably.

milestones.label: Larger, shaped samples retain superconductivity outside synthesis equipment
milestones.explanation: Repeatable production would have to exceed microgram quantities and yield macroscopic, shaped samples that remain superconducting outside synthesis equipment at room temperature and ordinary pressure. This would establish fabrication.

milestones.label: Operating limits and durability are measured
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish temperature, current and magnetic-field limits, retention time and survival through fabrication and repeated use under stated conditions. These would define which applications the material could serve.

uncertain: The proposed demonstration threshold may leave too little temperature margin for some applications.
It remains unclear whether the claimed atomic structure produces the high-pressure superconducting response.
Whether rapid pressure release can preserve superconductivity through warming and prolonged use remains open.

page.title: Bulk room-temperature superconductors at ambient pressure
page.definition: A bulk material can be made repeatedly and shaped into components that retain superconductivity at 300 K and atmospheric pressure outside synthesis equipment. It carries direct current with zero electrical resistance and exhibits the Meissner effect, expulsion of magnetic flux on entering the superconducting state.

goal.need: A 2026 PNAS perspective identifies superconducting magnets in about 40,000 MRI machines and calls for higher operating temperature together with high critical currents and magnetic fields. DOE’s 2006 workshop quantified the refrigeration overhead shown below. Ambient-pressure operation is an explicit goal of the University of Houston programme.

completion.title: Repeated fabrication yields bulk components superconducting at 300 K and atmospheric pressure.
completion.criterion: An independently reproduced synthesis produces the same identified bulk superconducting phase in separate runs. That material is fabricated into conductor or magnetic components that retain zero dc resistance within stated measurement resolution and Meissner flux expulsion in a sufficiently small applied field at 300 K and measured atmospheric pressure, outside synthesis equipment. Repeated fabrication preserves these properties through component testing. High-pressure synthesis followed by recovery qualifies.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback combining published temperature and pressure goals, superconductivity diagnostics, and the stated industrial-production objective.
completion.basis: Searches of DOE’s 2006 workshop report, the 2026 PNAS programme, IEC 61788 scopes and prize criteria found no joint temperature-pressure-fabrication acceptance test. This fallback adopts DOE’s nominal 300 K and the developer’s atmospheric-pressure goal. Repeatable component fabrication operationalises the industrial-production objective. No universal production-quantity, component-size, current-density or lifetime minimum was found.

milestones.title: A bulk material superconducts above 77 K at atmospheric pressure.
milestones.criterion: A bulk sample exhibits superconductivity above liquid nitrogen’s boiling point, approximately 77 K, at atmospheric pressure, with electrical and magnetic evidence. Wu and colleagues’ paper published on 2 March 1987 reports an 80–93 K transition in Y–Ba–Cu–O bars measuring 1 × 0.5 × 4 mm. The paper gives no total specimen count.
milestones.set_by: The superconductivity community’s liquid-nitrogen-temperature benchmark, documented by the National Academy of Sciences in Science at the Frontier, chapter 10.
milestones.threshold_quote: a material that would be superconducting at a temperature above 77 K

milestones.title: A pressure-quenched material retains a resistive-transition onset above 150 K at atmospheric pressure.
milestones.criterion: A pressure-enhanced phase retains an onset transition temperature above 150 K after rapid pressure release, using the resistance-derivative onset definition in Deng and colleagues’ protocol. Their paper published on 9 March 2026 studies five Hg-1223 specimens from three crystals. One specimen released from 18.9 GPa at 4.2 K showed 151 K on warming and 150 K on cooling. Separate stability measurements found retention for at least three days at 77 K and degradation above 200 K. Science News reports that explicit zero resistance was absent from the demonstration.
milestones.set_by: Deng and colleagues’ published pressure-quench protocol. Its target was written for HgBa2Ca2Cu3O8+δ, abbreviated Hg-1223. This milestone tracks the pressure-recovery route.

milestones.title: Independent laboratories reproduce bulk superconductivity at 300 K and atmospheric pressure.
milestones.criterion: Independent synthesis reproduces one identified bulk phase with zero dc resistance and small-field Meissner flux expulsion at 300 K and measured atmospheric pressure. Song and colleagues report 13 runs with onsets of 271–298 K at 195–266 GPa in their preprint revised on 6 October 2025. Direct Meissner measurements remain outstanding. Semenok and colleagues’ preprint revised on 20 August 2026 reports seven unsuccessful alloy-precursor syntheses at 250–280 GPa and no superconductivity at 245–300 K. Both cited versions are preprints without peer review.
milestones.set_by: Community conventions for superconductivity diagnostics, summarised by the University of Zurich, and independent experimental corroboration, documented by the American Physical Society. The operating target combines DOE’s nominal 300 K with the University of Houston’s ambient-pressure goal.
milestones.threshold_quote: It must conduct electricity without resistance, and it must expel the magnetic field from its bulk.

milestones.title: A fabricated bulk component superconducts at 300 K and atmospheric pressure.
milestones.criterion: A conductor or magnetic component fabricated from the identified bulk phase exhibits zero dc resistance within stated measurement resolution and small-field Meissner flux expulsion at 300 K and measured atmospheric pressure, outside synthesis equipment. The superconducting properties survive the fabrication sequence and component testing.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback. Searches of DOE’s workshop report, the 2026 PNAS programme and IEC 61788 scopes found no acceptance test for a fabricated bulk component operating superconductively at 300 K and atmospheric pressure. This test applies the published operating goals and superconductivity diagnostics after fabrication.

not_found: No published joint acceptance test for room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductivity and repeatable bulk-component fabrication was found.
No universal minimum production quantity, component dimensions, operating current density or room-temperature lifetime was found for this capability.
No independently replicated 300 K ambient-pressure bulk material or qualifying fabricated-component result was located through 14 November 2026.
